\section{Introduction}
Tea is among the most widely consumed beverages worldwide, and the
area under tea cultivation has expanded steadily in subtropical Asia.
Tea plants preferentially absorb ammonium, and the nitrification of
ammonium-based fertilisers releases protons into the rhizosphere.

Repeated surveys report that soils in a tea garden acidify faster than
adjacent forest or cropland soils. The consequences for the tea garden
soil microbiome are less well documented: acidification reshapes
bacterial community composition, but the trajectory across decades of
cultivation is rarely measured directly.

Here we use a chronosequence approach, sampling three tea garden sites
of 5, 18, and 34 years of continuous cultivation together with an
adjacent uncultivated reference plot, to quantify how soil chemistry
and the bacterial community co-vary with cultivation age.

\section{Materials and Methods}
The study tea plantation is located in the western hills of Shizuoka
Prefecture. Within the tea plantation we selected blocks planted in
1991, 2008, and 2020, sharing the same parent material and slope
aspect. An adjacent secondary forest served as the reference.

In each block of the tea plantation, five composite samples of the top
0--15~cm mineral soil were collected along a diagonal transect in
October 2025. Soil pH was measured in a 1:2.5 soil-to-water slurry,
and exchangeable aluminium was extracted with 1~M KCl and titrated.

Bacterial community composition was profiled by sequencing the V4
region of the 16S rRNA gene. Soil organic matter was determined by
loss on ignition at 550~$^\circ$C. Statistical differences among
cultivation ages were tested with a permutational analysis of variance.

\section{Results and Discussion}
Soil pH declined from 5.6 in the reference plot to 4.1 in the oldest
tea garden block, while exchangeable aluminium increased nearly
fourfold. Soil organic matter showed no monotonic trend with
cultivation age.

Bacterial diversity in the tea plantation decreased with cultivation
age, driven mainly by the loss of acid-sensitive taxa. The relative
abundance of Acidobacteria rose from 12\% in the youngest tea garden
to 29\% in the oldest, mirroring the pattern reported for other
acidified plantation soils.

The co-variation of chemistry and community composition suggests that
the pH decline in the tea plantation, rather than fertiliser input per
se, is the dominant filter on the bacterial community. Liming trials
in the oldest tea garden are planned to test this interpretation.
